title: Interlocked, compare-and-swap and the memory model
summary: Atomic operations, the compare-and-swap retry loop, why a plain flag can be invisible to another thread, and what volatile really promises.

steps.title: One CPU instruction instead of a lock
body: `Interlocked` turns a read-modify-write on **one** variable into a single atomic CPU instruction (`lock xadd`, `lock cmpxchg` on x64;
`ldadd`/`cas` or an `ldxr`/`stxr` loop on ARM64). No thread can get between the read and the write, and no thread ever blocks.
- `Interlocked.Increment(ref n)`, `Decrement`, `Add(ref n, k)`: counters and sequence numbers.
- `Interlocked.Exchange(ref x, v)`: swap in a new value, get the old one (hand-offs, "take the batch").
- `Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref x, newValue, expected)`: write `newValue` **only if** `x` still equals `expected`; always returns
what `x` was. That one primitive (compare-and-swap, CAS) builds everything else lock-free.
In the card, the increments are atomic (the green **A**): every interleaving gives 2.

steps.explain: The first call finds 5 as expected, writes 9, and returns the 5 it saw. The second expects 5 but finds 9: it writes nothing and returns 9. Comparing the return value with `expected` tells you whether your write happened.

steps.title: The compare-and-swap loop
body: To apply any function atomically to one variable: read it, compute the new value, and CAS it in; if someone changed it meanwhile,
**retry** with the fresh value.
```csharp fragment
public void Offer(int score)
int seen = Volatile.Read(ref _best);
while (score > seen)
int actual = Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref _best, score, seen);
if (actual == seen) return;      // our write won
seen = actual;                   // someone else wrote first: look again
Lock-free code never blocks, but it is easy to get subtly wrong and it does not compose: two variables that must change together
need a lock (or one immutable object swapped as a whole, next lesson). Use it for hot counters and single references; prefer `lock`
everywhere else.

steps.prompt: Put one attempt of the compare-and-swap loop in order.
lines: If it returned `seen`, the write happened: stop
Otherwise use the returned value as the new `seen` and go round again

steps.title: Memory model basics: visibility and reordering
body: Atomicity is half the story. The other half: **when does another thread see a write**, and in what order?
The C# compiler, the JIT and the CPU may **reorder** and **cache** memory operations as long as the *current* thread cannot tell.
Another thread can. The classic bug:
```csharp fragment
bool _stop;                          // set to true by another thread
void Worker() { while (!_stop) { } } // the JIT may read _stop once and loop forever
- `volatile bool _stop;` or `Volatile.Read(ref _stop)` forces a fresh read each time and keeps later reads from moving before it.
- `lock`, `Interlocked.*`, `Volatile.*`, `Task`/`await` hand-offs and `SemaphoreSlim` all include the **memory barriers** needed, so code
that uses them correctly does not need `volatile` too.
- x64 CPUs reorder little (a store can pass a later load); **ARM64** (Graviton and Ampere servers, Apple silicon, Windows on Arm)
reorders much more. Lock-free code "tested on my laptop" can fail the week you move to ARM servers.
The interleaving card cannot show reordering: it runs one step at a time, in order. That is why the advice is to use `lock`,
`Interlocked`, `Lazy<T>` and the concurrent collections, and to treat hand-written lock-free code as an expert job.

steps.prompt: Match each tool to what it guarantees.
pairs: one thread at a time in the block, and its writes are visible to the next owner
an atomic read-add-write on one variable
a fresh read that later reads and writes cannot move before
the factory runs once, and every thread sees the finished object

steps.prompt: A background worker polls `while (!_cancelled) DoChunk();` where `_cancelled` is a plain `bool` field set by `Stop()` on another thread. In Release builds it sometimes never stops. Which fix is best?
options: Replace the flag with a `CancellationToken` and check `ct.IsCancellationRequested` (or throw)
steps.explain: `CancellationToken` is built for exactly this: correct visibility, and the same token stops awaits and I/O. `volatile bool` also fixes the visibility bug, but a token is the idiomatic .NET answer. `Sleep` only happens to hide the bug.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: shared state
steps.body: The APIs seniors reach for when state is shared, roughly in order of preference.

toolkit.what: Protects any invariant over several fields. Short bodies, no await, no foreign code inside.
flags: the dedicated lock type; `object` works on older runtimes
toolkit.example: lock (_gate) { if (_balance < amount) return false; _balance -= amount; return true; }

toolkit.what: Atomic operations on a single int, long or reference; CAS for retry loops.
flags: swap and return the old value
toolkit.when: hot counters, ids, swapping one reference

toolkit.what: Run an initialiser once, on first use, safely. Wrap Task<T> for async: Lazy<Task<T>>.
flags: factory may run several times, first result wins
toolkit.when: singletons, expensive clients, caches of one item

toolkit.what: Copy-on-write: readers take the current immutable snapshot with no lock; writers CAS in a new one.
toolkit.when: read-mostly data: config, routing tables, feature flags

steps.title: A lock-free high score
prompt: Write a class **`HighScore`** with **`void Offer(int score)`**, which keeps the highest score offered so far, and **`int Best`**
(starts at 0). Use a **compare-and-swap loop** (`Interlocked.CompareExchange`), not a lock.
**How it is checked:** three threads offer 7, 9 and 3 under every interleaving; `Best` must end at 9.
hints: Read the current best into `seen`. While your score is higher, try `CompareExchange(ref _best, score, seen)`.
If it returns `seen`, you won; otherwise set `seen` to what it returned and loop again (the loop ends when someone wrote a higher score).
